n: Zephaniah gives an unusually long family line, reaching back four generations to “Hizkiah” — likely King Hezekiah. He prophesied under King Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before Josiah’s great reforms.

f.g: His name means “Jehovah has hidden” or “Jehovah treasures” — fitting for a book about being hidden in the day of wrath (2:3).
Probably King Hezekiah of Judah (about 715–686 BC).

n: The book opens with a sweeping warning: the Lord will sweep away everything from the face of the land.
People, animals, birds, and fish will be swept away — a reversal of Creation’s order. The idols that make people stumble will go with the wicked.

f.g: Idols or ruins — things that cause people to fall.

n: Judgment will focus on Judah and Jerusalem. God will remove every trace of Baal worship and the idolatrous priests.
He will cut off those who worship the stars on rooftops, and those who swear by the Lord and by Milcom at the same time — trying to serve two masters.

f.g: Milcom (or Molech), the national god of Ammon.

n: Also those who have turned away from the Lord and those who simply never bother to seek Him. Indifference is a form of rejection.

f.w: those that have not sought the LORD

n: Be silent before the Lord! His day is near. He has prepared a “sacrifice” and invited guests — but the shocking twist is that Judah itself is the sacrifice.

f.w: Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD

f.g: Consecrated His guests — perhaps the invading armies.

n: On that day God will punish the officials, the royal family, and those who dress in foreign styles — a sign of adopting pagan ways.

f.g: Foreign clothing, perhaps worn in pagan worship.

n: He will punish those who leap over the threshold (a pagan superstition) and fill their masters’ houses with violence and fraud.
Cries will rise from Jerusalem’s Fish Gate, wailing from the newer Second Quarter, and crashing from the hills — the city falling district by district.

f.g: The Mishneh, or “Second Quarter,” a newer part of Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:14).

n: Wail, you who live in the market district! All the traders and money handlers will be wiped out.

f.g: “The Mortar” — a hollow market district in Jerusalem.
Literally “people of Canaan,” a term used for traders.

n: God will search Jerusalem with lamps to find the complacent — those like wine left too long on its dregs, who think, “God won’t do anything, good or bad.”

f.g: Like wine left on its sediment — thick, stagnant, complacent.

f.w: The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil

n: Their wealth will be plundered and their homes destroyed. They will build and plant but never enjoy the results — covenant curses coming true.

f.w: build houses, but not inhabit them

n: The great day of the Lord is near and coming fast. Even warriors will cry bitterly.

f.w: The great day of the LORD is near

n: A famous description: a day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness, and clouds. The Latin hymn “Dies Irae” (“Day of Wrath”) takes its name from this verse.

f.w: That day is a day of wrath
f.g: In Latin, “Dies irae, dies illa” — the opening of a medieval hymn based on this verse.

f.w: a day of darkness and gloominess

n: A day of trumpet blasts and battle cries against fortified cities and high towers.
People will stumble like the blind because of their sin; their lives will be treated as worthless as dust.
Silver and gold won’t save them on that day. God’s jealous fire will consume the land. Wealth cannot buy deliverance from judgment.

f.w: Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them

f.g: Zeal — God’s passionate commitment to His covenant.
